(CNN) -- The world's wildlife has declined by 27 percent since 1970 because of the human impact on the environment, the World Wildlife Fund said Friday. These two adult frilled-neck lizards are threatened species and are bred in captivity in Australia. The WWF's latest Living Planet Index shows terrestrial, freshwater and marine species all suffered declines in their populations between 1970 and 2005, with freshwater species experiencing the biggest drop. The index is included in a report called "2010 and Beyond: Rising to the Biodiversity Challenge," which the WWF prepared for an international biodiversity conference in Germany later this month. "No one can escape the impact of biodiversity loss because reduced global diversity translates quite clearly into fewer new medicines, greater vulnerability to natural disasters, and greater effects from global warming," said James Leape, director-general of WWF International. The Living Planet Index measured 4,000 populations of 1,477 vertebrate species, which the WWF says is a good indicator of overall biodiversity trends. Terrestrial species in both temperate and tropical areas fell by an average of 25 percent during the 35-year period, the WWF said. Marine species fell by 28 percent in the same period, with a dramatic decline between 1995 and 2005, the WWF said. "Many marine ecosystems are changing rapidly under human influence, and one recent study estimates that more than 40 percent of the world's ocean area is strongly affected by human activities while few areas remain untouched," the WWF report said. Freshwater species in both temperate and tropical regions fell by 29 percent between 1970 and 2003. The WWF said that is especially significant because despite covering only about 1 percent of the total land surface of the planet, inland waters are home to more than 40,000 vertebrate species. In tropical regions, freshwater species were especially hard-hit; the index shows they suffered a 35-percent drop between 1970 and 2000. The WWF said it had insufficient data to chart tropical freshwater species beyond 2000 and temperate freshwater species beyond 2003. The causes of the declines are varied but ultimately stem from human demands on the biosphere, such as consumption of natural resources or the displacement of ecosystems, the WWF said. The dominant threat to marine life is overexploitation -- harvesting or killing animals or plants beyond the species' capacity to replace itself, the WWF said. Overfishing is one example. Overexploitation is also a threat to terrestrial species, according to the report, which cites the hunting of tropical forest mammals. Overharvesting of timber is also a major factor, it said. Invasive species, whether introduced deliberately or not, are another threat, especially in freshwater ecosystems, where they are thought to be the main cause of extinction among endemic species, the WWF said. Pollution and overall climate change are other factors causing a loss of biodiversity, it said. The WWF called on governments attending this month's conference to take urgent action to reduce the rate of loss by 2010. It wants governments to establish protected areas, particularly those areas important for food security, water supply, medicine, and disaster mitigation, and to commit to zero deforestation by 2020.

(CNN) — Human pressure on the environment has caused global wildlife to fall by 27 percent since 1970, the World Wildlife Fund said Friday.

Two adult frilled-neck lizards, a threatened species, are being raised in captivity in Australia.

According to the WWF’s newest Living Planet Index, populations of land, freshwater and ocean species all decreased between 1970 and 2005, with freshwater wildlife showing the steepest losses. The index appears in a report titled “2010 and Beyond: Rising to the Biodiversity Challenge,” prepared by the WWF for an international biodiversity meeting scheduled to take place in Germany later this month.

James Leape, director-general of WWF International, warned that everyone is affected by the decline in biodiversity. He said a less diverse natural world means fewer potential new medicines, increased exposure to natural disasters, and more severe consequences from global warming.

The Living Planet Index examined 4,000 populations belonging to 1,477 vertebrate species. The WWF said this provides a strong measure of broader biodiversity trends.

Over the 35-year span studied, land-based species in both temperate and tropical regions dropped by an average of 25 percent, the WWF reported. Ocean species declined by 28 percent over the same period, with the sharpest fall occurring between 1995 and 2005.

The WWF report said many marine environments are undergoing fast changes because of human activity. It cited a recent study estimating that more than 40 percent of the world’s ocean area is heavily influenced by people, while very few marine areas remain unaffected.

Freshwater species in temperate and tropical zones declined by 29 percent between 1970 and 2003. The WWF said this is particularly important because inland waters make up only about 1 percent of Earth’s land surface, yet support more than 40,000 vertebrate species.

Freshwater wildlife in tropical areas was hit especially hard. The index found a 35 percent decline in those species between 1970 and 2000. The WWF said it did not have enough information to track tropical freshwater species after 2000 or temperate freshwater species after 2003.

The reasons for the losses differ, but the WWF said they all ultimately come from human pressure on the biosphere, including the use of natural resources and the disruption or replacement of ecosystems.

For marine life, the leading danger is overexploitation, the WWF said. That means taking or killing animals or plants faster than the species can replenish itself; overfishing is one example.

The report said overexploitation also threatens land animals, pointing to the hunting of mammals in tropical forests. Excessive timber harvesting is another major contributor.

Invasive species, whether brought in intentionally or accidentally, are also a serious danger. The WWF said they are especially harmful in freshwater systems, where they are believed to be the main driver of extinctions among species found only in those areas.

Pollution and broader climate change are additional causes of biodiversity decline, the report said.

The WWF urged governments participating in this month’s conference to act quickly to slow the rate of biodiversity loss by 2010. It called for the creation of protected areas, especially places essential for food security, water supplies, medicine and disaster reduction, and asked governments to pledge to end deforestation completely by 2020.

In addition, damaged ecosystems are less able to store carbon and regulate climate, which can worsen the impacts of global warming.

Marine ecosystems are also undergoing rapid changes as a result of human influence. Together, these trends show that human activity is reshaping life on Earth at a global scale, making conservation and sustainable resource use increasingly urgent.

Human activity is placing unprecedented pressure on the natural world, and a major assessment by the World Wide Fund for Nature warns that wildlife populations have declined sharply over the past several decades. According to the WWF’s Living Planet Index, which examined about 4,000 populations from 1,477 vertebrate species, animals in forests, grasslands, rivers, lakes, wetlands, oceans, and coastal areas have all been affected by the growing human footprint.

The index found that, since 1970, monitored wildlife populations have fallen by an average of 27 percent. The decline reflects the combined effects of habitat destruction, pollution, overexploitation, invasive species, and climate change. As human populations have expanded and consumption has increased, natural habitats have been cleared or degraded for agriculture, logging, mining, urban development, roads, dams, and industry. These changes have reduced the space, food sources, and breeding grounds that many species need to survive.

Freshwater ecosystems have suffered the most severe losses. Species living in rivers, lakes, and wetlands are especially vulnerable because these environments are heavily affected by water extraction, dam construction, pollution, drainage, and changes in land use. Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals that depend on freshwater habitats have been hit hard as waterways are altered or contaminated. The report’s findings suggest that freshwater biodiversity is among the most threatened on the planet.

The decline is not only a concern for wildlife. Biodiversity supports essential systems that human societies rely on every day. Healthy ecosystems help purify water, pollinate crops, maintain fertile soils, regulate disease, and provide food and livelihoods. Many medicines have also been developed from compounds found in plants, animals, and microorganisms, meaning the loss of species could reduce opportunities for future medical discoveries.

Wildlife and intact ecosystems also play a crucial role in protecting people from natural disasters. Forests can reduce flooding and landslides, wetlands can absorb storm surges, and coral reefs can help shield coastlines from waves. When these natural defenses are damaged or destroyed, communities may become more exposed to extreme weather and other hazards.

The report also highlights the connection between biodiversity and climate stability. Forests, oceans, wetlands, and grasslands store large amounts of carbon and help regulate the Earth’s climate. As ecosystems are degraded, their ability to absorb carbon dioxide and buffer climate change is weakened. At the same time, climate change itself adds further stress to wildlife populations by altering temperatures, rainfall patterns, migration routes, and food availability.

The WWF’s findings serve as a warning that the loss of wildlife is part of a broader environmental crisis. Protecting biodiversity will require stronger conservation efforts, more sustainable use of land and water, reduced pollution, action on climate change, and changes in how societies produce and consume resources. Without significant action, the continued decline of wildlife could undermine the health of ecosystems and the well-being of future generations.

**WWF report: Global wildlife populations down 27% since 1970**

Global populations of wild animals have fallen by an estimated 27 percent since 1970, largely because of human pressure on the planet’s ecosystems, according to a report from the World Wide Fund for Nature.

The findings, drawn from WWF’s **Living Planet Index**, point to a broad decline in biodiversity as forests are cleared, wetlands drained, fisheries overexploited and greenhouse gas emissions alter habitats. The index tracks trends in populations of hundreds of vertebrate species — including mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish — as a measure of the health of the natural world.

WWF said the decline reflects the growing ecological footprint of humanity, including expanding agriculture, urban development, pollution, deforestation and the intensive use of freshwater and marine resources.

“Wildlife populations are an indicator of the state of the ecosystems on which people also depend,” the group said in its report, warning that continued losses could undermine food supplies, clean water, climate stability and livelihoods.

The Living Planet Index does not mean that all wildlife has declined by exactly 27 percent, nor that 27 percent of species have disappeared. Rather, it measures average changes in monitored animal populations over time. Some species and regions have fared worse than others, particularly freshwater systems, which are often highly vulnerable to dam construction, water extraction, pollution and habitat fragmentation.

The report was released as governments, scientists and conservation groups gathered for an international biodiversity conference aimed at slowing the accelerating loss of species and ecosystems. Delegates were expected to discuss stronger conservation targets, expanded protected areas and measures to reduce the human impacts driving habitat destruction and species decline.

Environmental groups said the WWF findings added urgency to negotiations, arguing that previous commitments to protect nature have often fallen short because of weak enforcement, inadequate funding and competing economic pressures.

Biodiversity experts say reversing the trend will require more than setting aside parks and reserves. They point to the need for sustainable agriculture, better fisheries management, restoration of degraded habitats, reduced pollution and action on climate change.

WWF said the report should serve as a warning that the planet’s natural systems are being depleted faster than they can recover.

“The message is clear,” the group said. “Human activity is placing unprecedented pressure on wildlife and the ecosystems that sustain life.”

---

# Wildlife Populations Have Plunged 73% Since 1970, WWF Report Warns

Global wildlife populations have fallen by an average of 73% in just 50 years, according to the World Wildlife Fund’s latest Living Planet Index, a stark warning that ecosystems essential to human life are being pushed toward dangerous tipping points.

The index, produced by WWF and the Zoological Society of London, tracks nearly 35,000 populations of more than 5,000 vertebrate species, including mammals, birds, fish, reptiles and amphibians. Its latest findings show that monitored wildlife populations declined dramatically between 1970 and 2020, with freshwater species suffering the steepest losses.

Freshwater populations dropped by an average of 85%, while terrestrial populations fell by 69% and marine populations by 56%, the report found.

The most severe regional decline was recorded in Latin America and the Caribbean, where monitored wildlife populations fell by 95%. Africa saw a 76% decline, while Asia and the Pacific recorded a 60% drop. North America and Europe and Central Asia also saw declines, though at lower levels, following decades of earlier environmental degradation before the index’s baseline year.

## Overfishing, habitat loss and invasive species among key drivers

WWF said the causes of biodiversity loss are varied but overwhelmingly linked to human activity.

Habitat destruction and degradation — including deforestation, agricultural expansion, wetland drainage and infrastructure development — remain the biggest threats to wildlife globally. As forests are cleared, rivers dammed and grasslands converted, species lose the places they need to feed, breed and migrate.

Overexploitation is another major factor. In marine ecosystems, overfishing has depleted fish stocks, disrupted food chains and damaged ocean habitats. Destructive fishing practices, such as bottom trawling, can also damage seafloor ecosystems that take decades or centuries to recover.

Invasive species are adding pressure in many regions. Non-native predators, plants, insects and pathogens can outcompete local species, spread disease and alter entire ecosystems. Island wildlife is especially vulnerable, as many native species evolved without defenses against introduced predators such as rats, cats and snakes.

Pollution, including plastics, pesticides, industrial chemicals and agricultural runoff, is also contributing to species declines. Climate change is increasingly amplifying these threats by shifting habitats, warming oceans, intensifying droughts and storms, and bleaching coral reefs.

WWF warned that biodiversity loss is not only an environmental crisis but also a direct threat to people. Healthy ecosystems provide food, clean water, pollination, flood protection and climate regulation. As wildlife populations fall and ecosystems weaken, those natural services become less reliable.

## Report warns of ecological tipping points

The report highlights the risk of “tipping points” — thresholds beyond which ecosystems may shift suddenly and irreversibly.

Scientists have long warned that the Amazon rainforest, for example, could reach a point where deforestation and warming cause large areas to dry out and transform into savanna-like landscapes. Such a shift would threaten countless species, release vast amounts of stored carbon and disrupt rainfall patterns across South America.

Coral reefs face similar risks as ocean temperatures rise. Mass bleaching events have become more frequent, threatening ecosystems that support marine biodiversity and the livelihoods of hundreds of millions of people.

Freshwater systems are also under severe strain. Rivers, lakes and wetlands are among the most threatened ecosystems on Earth, affected by dams, water extraction, pollution, invasive species and climate-driven changes in rainfall.

## Governments urged to act faster

WWF said governments must move beyond promises and rapidly implement existing global biodiversity commitments, including the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework agreed in 2022. That agreement includes a target to conserve at least 30% of the world’s land, inland waters and oceans by 2030.

Recommended actions include:

- Expanding and effectively managing protected and conserved areas  
- Restoring degraded forests, wetlands, rivers, grasslands and coastal ecosystems  
- Ending or redirecting subsidies that harm nature, including those linked to overfishing, deforestation and unsustainable agriculture  
- Strengthening rules against illegal wildlife trade and destructive fishing practices  
- Improving biosecurity to prevent and manage invasive species  
- Cutting greenhouse gas emissions to limit climate-related biodiversity loss  
- Supporting Indigenous peoples and local communities, who steward many of the world’s most biodiverse areas  
- Increasing public and private finance for conservation and nature restoration  
- Transforming food systems to reduce habitat destruction, waste and pollution  

WWF also called for stronger integration of climate and biodiversity policy, arguing that neither crisis can be solved in isolation. Protecting forests, wetlands, mangroves and oceans can help store carbon while also preserving wildlife and supporting communities.

## ‘Nature is sending a distress signal’

The findings add to a growing body of evidence that the natural world is under extraordinary pressure. Scientists caution that the Living Planet Index does not measure the total number of animals lost, but rather the average change in monitored wildlife populations. Even so, the scale and consistency of the decline point to a broad deterioration in global biodiversity.

Conservation groups say recovery is still possible, but only if governments act urgently.

Species can rebound when habitats are protected, exploitation is reduced and ecosystems are restored. Examples include recovering populations of some whales after commercial whaling bans, improved fish stocks under stronger management, and the return of wildlife to restored wetlands and forests.

But WWF warned that the window for action is narrowing.

The report’s central message is clear: biodiversity loss is accelerating, human activity is the main driver, and governments have the tools to slow — and in some cases reverse — the damage. What remains uncertain is whether they will act quickly enough.

**Global wildlife decline deepens as WWF warns of “ecological credit crunch”**

*By Environmental News Desk*

Global biodiversity is continuing to decline at an alarming rate, with monitored populations of mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish falling sharply over recent decades, according to data cited by the World Wide Fund for Nature.

WWF’s Living Planet Index, which tracks trends in thousands of populations across **1,477 vertebrate species**, shows that wildlife abundance has dropped significantly since 1970, reflecting mounting pressure from habitat destruction, overexploitation, pollution, invasive species and climate change. The decline is especially severe in tropical regions, freshwater ecosystems and forests converted for agriculture, logging and infrastructure.

James Leape, then director general of WWF International, warned that the figures show humanity is drawing down nature’s capital faster than ecosystems can recover.

“We are consuming the resources that underpin our economies and our lives,” Leape said in WWF’s assessment of the global trend. He described the biodiversity crisis as an “ecological credit crunch,” arguing that the world has been living beyond the planet’s means by using forests, fisheries, soils and freshwater faster than they can be replenished.

The WWF findings add to growing evidence that the world has failed to halt biodiversity loss despite repeated international pledges. Conservation scientists say the decline of vertebrate populations is not only a measure of wildlife loss, but also a warning signal for the health of ecosystems that provide food, clean water, climate regulation and protection from natural disasters.

### Habitat loss remains leading threat

The most significant driver of biodiversity decline remains the destruction and fragmentation of habitats. Forests continue to be cleared for cattle ranching, soy, palm oil, timber and mining, while wetlands are drained and rivers dammed or polluted. Marine species face pressure from overfishing, warming seas and ocean acidification.

WWF and other conservation groups have called for a rapid expansion of protected areas, stronger enforcement against illegal logging and wildlife trade, and better management of landscapes where people and nature coexist.

The organization has urged governments to commit to **zero net deforestation by 2020**, warning that continued forest loss would undermine efforts to protect species and stabilize the climate. Forests are home to much of the world’s terrestrial biodiversity and absorb vast amounts of carbon dioxide, making them central to both conservation and climate policy.

Leape said reversing biodiversity decline would require governments and businesses to recognize the economic value of nature rather than treating ecosystems as expendable.

“The choice is not between development and conservation,” he said. “The question is whether development can continue if we destroy the natural systems on which it depends.”

### Protected areas seen as essential

Conservationists say well-managed protected areas remain one of the most effective tools for safeguarding biodiversity. But many existing reserves are too small, poorly funded or isolated from surrounding habitats. WWF has called for protected area networks that are ecologically representative, connected and supported by local communities.

The push for more protected areas includes forests, freshwater basins, grasslands, coral reefs and marine habitats. Scientists say protection must be paired with sustainable production outside reserve boundaries, including deforestation-free supply chains, responsible fisheries and restoration of degraded ecosystems.

WWF’s warning comes amid rising concern that biodiversity loss is becoming a systemic global risk, similar to climate change. As species disappear and ecosystems degrade, the consequences extend beyond wildlife: crop pollination declines, fisheries collapse, disease risks can rise and communities lose natural buffers against floods, droughts and storms.

The report’s message is clear, WWF says: halting biodiversity decline will require urgent action, including stronger protected areas, an end to deforestation, reduced overconsumption and policies that place nature at the center of economic planning.

In a report released before the United Nations biodiversity talks, WWF said many species are suffering as forests are cleared, oceans are overfished, rivers are altered and pollution spreads. The group said the demands people place on the planet are outstripping nature’s ability to recover.

WWF’s warning comes as representatives from governments, conservation groups and international organizations gather to discuss how to slow the loss of biodiversity — the variety of life on Earth, from plants and animals to the ecosystems that support them.

Conservationists say the decline of wildlife is not only an environmental issue, but also a threat to human well-being. Healthy ecosystems provide food, clean water, medicine, flood protection and climate regulation.

WWF said the greatest pressures on wildlife include destruction of habitat for agriculture and development, illegal and unsustainable hunting, overfishing, invasive species, pollution and the increasing effects of climate change.

The organization called on world leaders to expand protected areas, strengthen enforcement against wildlife crime, reduce greenhouse gas emissions and adopt more sustainable patterns of production and consumption.

Scientists have long warned that biodiversity is being lost at an accelerating rate. WWF said reversing the trend will require coordinated international action, as well as changes in how governments and industries manage land, water and natural resources.

The conference in Germany is expected to focus on whether countries are meeting global targets to reduce biodiversity loss and what additional measures are needed to protect threatened species and habitats.

Environmental groups say the stakes are high: without urgent action, they warn, the planet could lose more of the wildlife populations that help sustain life for both nature and people.
